\begin{abstract}

Gender quotas expand access to elected office, but their implications for officeholders' qualifications may vary across settings. We compare winners of women-reserved and open seats in rural Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Kerala and in Mumbai and Delhi, and combine these estimates with existing schooling studies. In our records, reserved-seat village heads in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh are `r fmt(ss$head_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(ss$head_gap[2], 0)` percentage points less likely to hold a university degree. Kerala's village ward members and councillors in Mumbai and Delhi show no consistent schooling deficit. These estimates distinguish the settings, although the urban intervals do not establish equivalence. Reserved-seat winners are `r fmt(es$occupation_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$occupation_gap[2], 0)` points more likely to report no occupation in the village, block and city offices with occupation records, and declare lower assets in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. In Mumbai and Delhi, they are `r fmt(ss$case_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(ss$case_gap[2], 0)` points less likely to face pending criminal charges. Qualification differences between reserved and open seats depend on both the attribute and the office.

\end{abstract}

# Introduction

Gender quotas broaden access to elected office. Whether they also change officeholders' qualifications matters for how representative government works. Local officials must interpret administrative rules, oversee expenditure, and negotiate with other officials [@auerbach]. Schooling and political experience may help them perform these tasks; economic resources may affect their independence. Yet these attributes need not move together, and none alone establishes how well an official governs. The question is which qualifications change when office is reserved for women.

Research on Indian village heads often finds that winners of women-reserved seats have less schooling and prior political experience than winners of open seats [@cd; @ban; @afridi]. That evidence has an important qualification. Women who enter politics can be positively selected relative to other women even when they have less schooling than male politicians. Evidence from Karnataka, for example, finds stronger selection on cognitive skills among female than male candidates relative to voters of their own gender [@moripublished]. The qualifications of elected officials depend both on the eligible population and on who enters and wins elections.

This leaves a puzzle. Is the schooling gap a common consequence of reservation, or does it depend on the opportunities and barriers women face in a particular political setting? Much of the existing evidence concerns village heads. It does not establish whether the same pattern holds among other rural officials or urban councillors. Nor does a schooling difference establish a broader qualification disadvantage: economic position and criminal records could follow different patterns.

We extend this literature by comparing qualifications across rural and urban offices in several Indian states. A common university-degree threshold makes the education comparisons easier to interpret across settings. Occupation, assets, age, and criminal records allow us to ask whether the education pattern extends to other attributes. We also synthesize the existing schooling evidence alongside our estimates, expressing differences in standard-deviation units, summarizing distinct settings separately, and counting overlapping samples once. The contribution is to establish how qualification differences vary across offices, settings, and attributes, rather than to infer a single ranking of leader quality.

Our analysis uses election records and candidate affidavits for rural councils in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Kerala and municipal councils in Mumbai and Delhi. We compare winners of women-reserved and open seats separately by state, election, and office; open seats can also elect women. The regressions include geographic and caste-reservation effects where the records permit them, with standard errors clustered geographically. A causal interpretation requires reservation to be as good as randomly assigned within the comparison groups. We also examine how missing qualifications limit conclusions about all winners.

The education results differ across settings. Among village heads in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, reserved-seat winners are `r fmt(ss$head_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(ss$head_gap[2], 0)` percentage points less likely to hold a university degree. Rajasthan also has a negative estimate among winners with classifiable education, but extensive missingness prevents an all-winner conclusion. Kerala's village ward members and the councillors of Mumbai and Delhi show no consistent graduate-share deficit, and their confidence intervals include zero. The urban intervals are too wide to establish equivalence. Comparing village ward members in Bihar and Kerala preserves the contrast, so it is not solely a difference between heads and members. Differences in women's education and access to political life are possible explanations, but offices, election years, and data coverage also vary across settings. Our design cannot separate those explanations.

Other attributes follow different patterns. Across the village, block, and city offices with occupation records, reserved-seat winners are `r fmt(es$occupation_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$occupation_gap[2], 0)` points more likely to report no occupation, including where the estimated education differences are small. They also declare fewer assets in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. In Mumbai and Delhi, however, they are `r fmt(ss$case_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(ss$case_gap[2], 0)` points less likely to face a pending criminal case. The lower prevalence of charges is a potentially favorable difference, although charges are not convictions and our records do not establish its consequences for governing performance. Reservation is associated with different changes in different qualifications; the schooling evidence alone does not describe that pattern.

# Related literature

## Evidence on officials' qualifications

The most consistent evidence on qualifications concerns schooling among village heads. Surveys generally find less schooling among winners of women-reserved seats. The comparisons assembled in Table \ref{tab:literature} report lower years of schooling in West Bengal and South India [@cd, Table 3; @beaman, Table II; @ban, Table 9], lower secondary-school attainment in a national village panel and Andhra Pradesh [@deininger, Table 3; @afridi, Table 2]. These studies combine descriptive and adjusted comparisons and measure different schooling outcomes. We synthesize differences in qualifications, without treating the estimates as a common causal effect.

The schooling measures range from years of education to completion of secondary school. We express these comparisons and our graduate-share estimates in standard-deviation units and compare the patterns across settings in Section \ref{sec:synthesis}. Not every relevant study supplies an eligible comparison. In Tamil Nadu, female and male presidents have relatively similar reported schooling distributions [@gajwani, p. 246]. In Maharashtra, female sarpanches have fewer years of schooling, but the study compares women and men, including a woman elected without a current reservation, rather than reserved and open seats [@priebe, Table 2 and note 6].

Schooling is one component of preparation for office. Reserved-seat leaders also have less prior political experience in West Bengal, South India, and Andhra Pradesh [@cd, Table 3; @ban, Table 9; @afridi, Table 2]. Local officials must also understand administrative procedures, obtain information, and negotiate with other officials. Village heads' responsibilities for budgets, public works, and benefit allocation make these skills relevant [@auerbach, pp. 708–710; @joshi, p. 56]. In Tamil Nadu, female presidents score `r fmt(-lit_value("gajwani", "female_vs_male"), 1)` points lower on a 19-question test of panchayat rules and duties after adjustment for schooling and other observed characteristics. They also report less contact with higher-level officials [@gajwani, Tables 5–6]. The knowledge coefficient is an adjusted gender comparison, not an estimate of the causal contribution of schooling. It nevertheless shows why similar educational attainment need not imply similar preparation for governing.

## Possible mechanisms

Lower schooling relative to open-seat winners can coexist with positive selection relative to other women. In South India, reserved-seat leaders are wealthier and more politically informed than eligible women [@ban, Table 9]. Evidence from Karnataka similarly finds that female candidates are more positively selected on cognitive skills relative to female voters than male candidates are relative to male voters [@moripublished]. For Bihar's 2016 and 2021 elections, @bamezai report lower schooling among reserved-seat winners near reservation thresholds, using local citizens as the benchmark. We discuss that evidence separately because it measures a local effect on citizen-standardized schooling, not the broad winner comparison synthesized here. Differences between eligible populations and differences in whom elections draw from each population are distinct potential sources of qualification gaps. Our winner records cannot separate them.

Bhavnani, Huidobro and Prillaman's October 2024 draft also reports lower schooling in women-reserved seats. For Odisha's 2022 election, the adjusted difference is `r fmt(bhavnani$estimate[bhavnani$sample == "Odisha 2022" & bhavnani$caste == "Non-SC/ST"], 2)` years among seats without SC/ST reservation [@bhavnani, Table 2, column 4]. Their claims about equal or higher quality concern household-wealth residuals and education relative to one's identity group. Those measures address different questions from attained schooling and do not directly measure governing performance. The appendix reconstructs the caste-specific schooling comparisons.

Gender quotas can also change representation along dimensions other than gender. In the Rural Economic and Demographic Survey, reservation for women reduces high-caste candidacy and representation; differences in women's mobility across caste groups provide a possible explanation [@cassan, Tables 1–2 and 9–11]. Education, assets, caste, and family political experience may therefore change together. Our controls for a seat's caste-reservation category distinguish institutional categories, but do not isolate the mechanisms through which candidates enter or voters choose among them.

Experience can alter these differences after entry into office. In Andhra Pradesh, councils reserved for women initially show more leakage and implementation problems in a public employment program, but audit outcomes improve as female leaders accumulate experience [@afridi]. Evidence from South India also links political experience to women's performance in office [@ban]. Among citizens in Uttar Pradesh, gaps in political participation persist after accounting for education, political knowledge, assets, and restrictions on mobility, suggesting that observed qualifications do not exhaust the barriers to participation [@iyermani]. Entry qualifications and the opportunities to acquire governing experience are distinct objects of study.

Formal office also differs from authority over decisions. Research on rural councils documents limits on women's participation in deliberation and the involvement of male relatives in everyday governance [@heinze; @amar; @karekurvesood]. Publicly reported work on collective family governance finds family involvement in both male- and female-led councils, alongside lower political authority for women [@familypolitics]. These findings caution against interpreting every family connection as evidence of substitution for the elected official. Our occupation and asset measures describe economic position; they do not directly measure control over household resources or the exercise of political authority. A declaration of no occupation may also encompass substantial unpaid work.

## Qualifications and governing performance

The association between formal qualifications and performance is itself an empirical question. More educated council heads in South India allocate benefits differently, including greater targeting to landless households [@besleyrewards, Tables 4–5]. Graduates who narrowly win Indian state assembly elections increase constituency night-time-light growth [@jaineducation, Table 2]. Evidence from national leaders, US legislators, and Brazilian mayors, however, does not establish a general performance advantage for college graduates [@carneslupu]. Other attributes have their own implications: narrowly electing legislators who face criminal charges reduces growth and road provision in India [@prakash], while younger Italian mayors facing reelection exhibit larger electoral budget cycles [@alesinaage, Tables 5–7]. None of these findings warrants combining schooling, age, wealth, and criminal records into a single ranking of leader quality.

The effects of reservation on governance extend beyond the credentials of the elected official. In West Bengal and Rajasthan, reservation changes public investment toward goods requested by women [@cdpublished, Table V]. Within India, the evidence varies by outcome and setting. Tamil Nadu's female-led councils build fewer schools and roads [@gajwani, Tables 7–8], while a broader village survey finds greater public-goods availability and fewer reported bribes despite lower satisfaction with female leaders [@duflotopalova, Tables 2–4]. In Maharashtra, improvements in women's political participation coexist with mixed service-delivery differences [@priebe, Tables 4 and 6]. Repeated exposure to female leaders in West Bengal also raises girls' aspirations and educational attainment [@beamanaspirations, Tables 1–3]. These outcomes concern policy, participation, and longer-run opportunities, which our records of officeholders do not measure.

The unresolved question for this paper is how broadly the qualification differences documented among village heads extend across offices and attributes. We address that question with comparable measures where the administrative records permit them, while retaining separate estimates for each setting.

# Institutional setting, data, and empirical strategy

## Reserved seats and the comparison

Women-reserved seats restrict eligibility to women; open seats permit both women and men to contest. Gender reservation also operates within caste-reservation categories. These rules change eligibility, but their assignment procedures differ across jurisdictions. We therefore retain separate state, election, and office comparisons and make the identifying assumption explicit below. Differences across settings also reflect differences in offices, election years, and source coverage; they do not by themselves identify an effect of a state's social or institutional environment.

## Data sources

The administrative records come from state election repositories through [local_elections](https://github.com/in-rolls/local_elections), with input hashes, winner rules, exclusions and coding dictionaries saved in the repository. Bihar's winner is the highest vote-getter, an uncontested candidate, or the winner of a tie drawn by lot; seats whose results form cannot identify a winner are excluded. Kerala's records are of elected ward members, and their reservation refers to the ward even for members who later lead the council.

Bihar's 2021 records include age but not education. We obtain reservation status from the State Election Commission's feed for the 2021–2026 term and verify that it reproduces the Commission's count of women-reserved village-head seats. Kerala records education as free text; we classify recognized degrees and school qualifications and leave incomplete or unrecognized entries missing.

Mumbai's councillor records come from the Praja Foundation's report cards and affidavits, as deposited by @mumbaidata. Each councillor with a recorded age enters once per term.

The Delhi data cover the municipal elections of 2012, 2017, and 2022. Winners and assembly mapping for 2012 and 2017 come from Goyal's replication deposit [@delhigoyal]; for 2022, winners come from the OpenCity compilation of Lok Dhaba results and reservation from the State Election Commission's gazette [@delhi2022results; @delhi2022seats, Annexure B]. The 2012 reservation labels match the official schedule [@delhi2012seats, Annexures I–III]. Qualifications and pending cases come from each winner's MyNeta profile [@delhimyneta]; convictions are excluded from pending cases. We use these profiles to measure Delhi winners' education because the older deposited classifications disagree with the affidavits. The measurement appendix reports that comparison.

## Outcomes and samples

The main education outcome is whether the winner holds a university degree; the appendix also reports illiteracy. Unknown qualifications stay missing. Occupation is recorded in Rajasthan, Kerala and Delhi. A winner counts as having no occupation when the entry is nil, unemployed, homemaker or student; pensioners and every named trade or job count as an occupation, with the coding rules recorded in the accompanying analysis code.

Declared assets come from the nomination affidavits of Rajasthan's 2020 and Uttar Pradesh's 2021 village heads. We analyze declared assets on a logarithmic scale.

MyNeta's affidavit summaries record pending criminal cases in Mumbai and Delhi. Uttar Pradesh's 2021 affidavits instead provide an indicator of reported criminal history.

## Specification and inference

For each state, election and office, we estimate

\[
Y_i = \alpha + \beta R_i + \gamma_{g(i)} + \delta_{c(i)} + \epsilon_i,
\]

where $R_i$ indicates a seat reserved for women, $\gamma_{g(i)}$ is a block effect (a district effect where blocks are not recorded throughout) and $\delta_{c(i)}$ is an effect for the seat's caste-reservation class. For binary outcomes, $100\beta$ is the reserved-minus-open difference in percentage points among seats in the same block and caste class. It is the effect of reservation if reservation is as good as randomly assigned within those cells. Standard errors are clustered by block or district, and 95% intervals use a $t$ distribution with one fewer degree of freedom than there are clusters; Kerala's ward and district-member models have only `r num(get_result("Kerala", 2020, "gp_ward")$clusters)` clusters. Mumbai pools its 2012 and 2017 councils with administrative-ward and council effects, clustered by electoral ward, and has no caste-reservation control. Delhi uses assembly-constituency and caste-reservation effects in each election, clustered by assembly constituency.

## Combining the schooling evidence

The meta-analysis combines existing reserved-versus-open schooling comparisons with this paper's estimates. Years of schooling are expressed relative to their within-sample standard deviation. For binary schooling thresholds, we convert log odds ratios to the same approximate scale. Our threshold estimates use logistic regressions with the controls and clustering described above. This conversion assumes that the thresholds measure a common underlying schooling distribution; it does not make secondary completion and a university degree the same qualification.

We summarize published village-head comparisons, our northern village-head comparisons, and our Kerala ward-member and city comparisons separately. The model includes a mean for each group and random effects for settings and elections within settings. These groups describe the observed pattern; they do not identify the effects of urbanization, office, or women's opportunities. We retain one Birbhum study and exclude citizen-relative selection measures and local RD estimates. The appendix gives the conversion, model coverage, and an overall average for comparison.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

# Results

## Rural panchayats

### Village heads

Among village heads in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, winners of women-reserved seats are less likely to hold a university degree. In Bihar's 2016 election, the adjusted graduate-share difference is `r contrast(get_result("Bihar", 2016, "gp_head"))`. Uttar Pradesh shows the same direction in each election. Its estimated differences are `r contrast(get_result("Uttar Pradesh", 2010, "gp_head"))` in 2010, `r contrast(get_result("Uttar Pradesh", 2015, "gp_head"))` in 2015, and `r contrast(get_result("Uttar Pradesh", 2021, "gp_head"))` in 2021. The estimated deficit narrows over time, but all three intervals remain below zero. These are comparisons of the winners in each election, not changes in the qualifications of the same individuals.

```{r rural-heads-plot, fig.cap="Graduate-share differences among rural village heads, women-reserved minus open seats, with geography and caste-reservation effects. Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals clustered by geography. UP 2010 uses districts; other rows use blocks. Unclassified education, ambiguous winners and unknown reservation are excluded."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("figs/rural_heads.png"))
```

Rajasthan also has a negative education difference among village heads whose qualifications can be classified: `r contrast(get_result("Rajasthan", 2020, "gp_head"))`. Here, however, missing education changes the conclusion we can draw. Many records report only "Other," and the share with classifiable education differs between reserved and open seats. Allowing each unclassified winner to be either a graduate or a nongraduate yields an all-winner coefficient between `r fmt(raj_bounds$all_winners_lower * 100)` and `r fmt(raj_bounds$all_winners_upper * 100)` percentage points. This range allows substantial differences in either direction. The observed negative gap therefore describes the classified sample; it does not establish a graduate-share deficit among all Rajasthan village heads. These bounds address missing outcomes and do not incorporate sampling uncertainty.

### Bihar's other offices

The education difference in Bihar extends beyond village heads. The 2016 records cover `r num(nrow(report$settings$bihar_2016$analysis))` elected seats across six village, block, and district offices. Reserved-seat winners have lower graduate shares in every office, although the size of the difference varies. Among village ward members, the adjusted difference is `r contrast(bihar_ward)`; among block council members it is `r contrast(get_result("Bihar", 2016, "block_member"))`. The gap is thus present among council members as well as heads, rather than being confined to the village executive office.

```{r bihar-plot, fig.cap="Bihar 2016: graduate-share differences by office, women-reserved minus open seats, with block and caste-reservation effects (district effects for district council members). Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals clustered at that level."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("figs/bihar_2016_education.png"))
```

Reserved-seat village heads are also younger. The estimated age difference is `r fmt(-head_age(2016)$estimate)` years in 2016 and `r fmt(-head_age(2021)$estimate)` years in 2021 (95% CI `r fmt(-head_age(2021)$conf_high)` to `r fmt(-head_age(2021)$conf_low)`). The 2021 data cover `r num(nrow(report$settings$bihar_2021$analysis))` elected seats but contain no education measure, so they cannot establish whether the schooling gap persisted. Age describes another difference in who holds office; without records of prior political experience, it cannot establish that younger winners are less prepared to govern.

### Kerala

Kerala's village ward members show much smaller education differences. The adjusted graduate-share differences are `r contrast(get_result("Kerala", 2010, "gp_ward"))` in 2010, `r contrast(get_result("Kerala", 2015, "gp_ward"))` in 2015, and `r contrast(get_result("Kerala", 2020, "gp_ward"))` in 2020. Each interval includes zero, and none includes a deficit as large as the one estimated for Bihar's village ward members. Comparing this common office therefore preserves the contrast between Bihar and Kerala; the pattern is not simply a consequence of comparing northern heads with Kerala's council members.

```{r kerala-plot, fig.cap="Rural Kerala: graduate-share differences by election and office, women-reserved minus open seats, with caste-reservation effects. Block members use block effects and clustering; village and district members use districts. Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("figs/kerala_education.png"))
```

This result applies most clearly to village ward members, not to every Kerala office. For block council members, the estimated differences are negative in all three elections, and the 2010 interval excludes zero (`r contrast(get_result("Kerala", 2010, "block_member"))`). The district council estimates are also negative but substantially less precise. Moreover, these comparisons describe winners with classifiable education. The missing-outcome bounds for Kerala permit either sign, so small estimated gaps in the observed sample do not establish equal educational attainment among all elected officials.

## Urban councils

### Mumbai

Mumbai does not show the graduate-share deficit found among northern village heads. Across the 2012 and 2017 councils, the adjusted difference is `r contrast(mg)`. The point estimate favors reserved-seat winners, but its interval includes zero. Within the observed sample and regression specification, the interval permits a negligible disadvantage or a substantial advantage; it provides little support for a deficit of the magnitude observed among northern village heads.

```{r mumbai-plot, fig.cap="Mumbai councillors in the 2012 and 2017 councils: women-reserved minus open seats in graduate share, any pending case and declaring no tax ID (PAN), with administrative-ward and council effects. Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals clustered by electoral ward."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("figs/mumbai_quality.png"))
```

The difference in pending criminal cases is larger and more precisely estimated. Reserved-seat councillors are `r fmt(-100 * mc$estimate)` percentage points less likely to face a pending case (95% CI `r fmt(-100 * mc$conf_high)` to `r fmt(-100 * mc$conf_low)`). This is a difference in the prevalence of charges against elected officials. It does not measure convictions or establish how reservation affects misconduct or performance in office.

### Delhi

In Delhi, the estimated graduate-share differences are small, but their uncertainty is substantial. The estimated graduate-share differences are `r contrast(get_delhi(2012))` in 2012, `r contrast(get_delhi(2017))` in 2017, and `r contrast(get_delhi(2022))` in 2022. The estimates vary in sign, and all three intervals include sizable differences in both directions. The Delhi results therefore do not establish an education advantage or disadvantage, and they are too imprecise to establish equivalent graduate shares.

```{r delhi-plot, fig.cap="Delhi councillors by election: women-reserved minus open seats in graduate share, reporting no occupation and any pending case, with assembly-constituency and caste-reservation effects. Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals clustered by assembly constituency."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("figs/delhi_quality.png"))
```

Pending criminal cases show a more consistent pattern. The reserved-minus-open differences are `r contrast(get_delhi(2012, "any_criminal"))` in 2012, `r contrast(get_delhi(2017, "any_criminal"))` in 2017, and `r contrast(get_delhi(2022, "any_criminal"))` in 2022. All three intervals lie below zero. The sign also remains negative when every missing case indicator is allowed to be either zero or one, holding the regression design fixed. These bounds address incomplete records and do not incorporate sampling uncertainty. They also cannot establish the accuracy of declarations or the consequences of pending cases for governance. The urban evidence is consequently clearer about the lower prevalence of charges than about differences in educational attainment.

## Occupation, assets and criminal records

Differences in reported occupation extend to settings where the education estimates are close to zero. In Rajasthan, the share reporting no occupation is `r fmt(100 * es$rajasthan_occupation$estimate, 0)` percentage points higher among reserved-seat village heads (95% CI `r fmt(100 * es$rajasthan_occupation$conf_low, 0)` to `r fmt(100 * es$rajasthan_occupation$conf_high, 0)`). Among Kerala's village ward members, the estimated differences range from `r fmt(es$kerala_ward_occupation[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$kerala_ward_occupation[2], 0)` points across the three elections; among Delhi's councillors, they range from `r fmt(es$delhi_occupation[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$delhi_occupation[2], 0)` points. Thus, the small education differences in these settings coexist with large differences in reported occupation. Kerala's district council members show smaller occupation differences, ranging from `r fmt(es$kerala_district_occupation[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$kerala_district_occupation[2], 0)` points.

The occupation measure combines declarations of no work, unemployment, homemaking, and student status. It describes reported occupation, not the absence of productive activity or access to household resources. Coding "social worker" as missing rather than as an occupation changes no estimate by more than `r fmt(ceiling(es$social_shift), 0)` percentage points, so that particular coding choice does not account for the broad pattern. The records do not show whether women with no reported occupation control assets or exercise political authority independently.

Mumbai's records contain no occupation measure. The adjusted difference in the share declaring no tax identification number (PAN) is `r contrast(mp)`, with nondeclaration more common among reserved-seat winners. Nondeclaration occurs only in the 2012 council records. This is an additional difference in affidavit disclosure; it cannot substitute for a direct measure of employment or income.

Reserved-seat village heads declare fewer assets in both states with asset records. The estimates imply approximately `r fmt(-es$rajasthan_assets, 0)`% lower assets in Rajasthan (95% CI `r fmt(100 * (1 - exp(rajasthan_assets$conf_high)), 0)`% to `r fmt(100 * (1 - exp(rajasthan_assets$conf_low)), 0)`% lower) and `r fmt(-es$up_assets, 0)`% lower assets in Uttar Pradesh (95% CI `r fmt(100 * (1 - exp(up_assets$conf_high)), 0)`% to `r fmt(100 * (1 - exp(up_assets$conf_low)), 0)`% lower). The asset differences reinforce the evidence from occupation that reserved-seat winners occupy a different economic position. Affidavits record declared holdings, however, and do not establish who controls those resources.

The urban difference in pending cases does not have a clear counterpart in Uttar Pradesh's village-head records. Only `r fmt(es$up_crime_rate, 2)`% of winners with a known record report a criminal history. The adjusted reserved-minus-open difference is `r fmt(100 * es$up_crime$estimate, 2)` percentage points (95% CI `r fmt(100 * es$up_crime$conf_low, 2)` to `r fmt(100 * es$up_crime$conf_high, 2)`), leaving the direction uncertain. This outcome is reported criminal history, whereas the urban measure concerns pending cases, so differences across these settings also reflect the measures available. The appendix reports the full estimates and sample sizes.

## Schooling across the literature and our data \label{sec:synthesis}

The schooling evidence shows two broad patterns. The eligible published village-head comparisons and our northern village-head estimates all indicate less schooling among winners of women-reserved seats. Kerala's village ward members and the councillors of Mumbai and Delhi show no consistent deficit. Figure \ref{fig:combined-forest} displays the individual estimates and separate group summaries. A single average would obscure the distinction that motivates the comparison across settings.

On the approximate SD scale, the summary difference is `r fmt(schooling_groups$d[1], 2)` (95% CI `r fmt(schooling_groups$low[1], 2)` to `r fmt(schooling_groups$high[1], 2)`) among published village-head comparisons and `r fmt(schooling_groups$d[2], 2)` (`r fmt(schooling_groups$low[2], 2)` to `r fmt(schooling_groups$high[2], 2)`) among our northern village heads. The summary for Kerala and the two cities is `r fmt(schooling_groups$d[3], 2)` SD (`r fmt(schooling_groups$low[3], 2)` to `r fmt(schooling_groups$high[3], 2)`). We keep the two village-head groups separate because their measures and research designs differ. The Kerala and city summary is close to zero, but its interval allows modest differences in either direction, and the individual Delhi estimates are imprecise.

```{r combined-forest, fig.cap="Schooling differences, women-reserved minus open seats, combining the literature and this paper. Circles are individual estimates and diamonds are group means; bars show 95\\% confidence intervals. Years of schooling use pooled within-group SDs; binary thresholds use a log-odds conversion. Our estimates retain geography and reservation controls and clustered uncertainty. Group means come from a model with source/setting-group indicators and random effects for settings and elections within settings. Birbhum enters once; citizen-standardized RD estimates are excluded. Appendix A gives conversion assumptions and sensitivity checks.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("figs/forest_combined.png"))
```

The graduate-share deficit is larger among northern village heads than among Kerala's village ward members and the two cities' councillors. Pooling this paper's estimates with elections nested in settings, reserved-seat village heads in the northern states are `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern[1])` points less likely to hold a degree (95% CI `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern_high[1])` to `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern_low[1])`), against a difference of `r fmt(setting_meta$other_settings[1])` points (`r fmt(setting_meta$other_low[1])` to `r fmt(setting_meta$other_high[1])`) among Kerala's ward members and the two cities' councillors. The estimated difference between these groups is `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern_gap[1])` percentage points (95% CI `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern_gap_high[1])` to `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern_gap_low[1])`). Office, data source and election years vary along with setting, and the second group is one state and two cities. Replacing Bihar's village heads with its ward members, the office we observe in Kerala, still leaves a northern gap of `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern[3])` points.

The grouping summarizes a pattern in the observed comparisons, not two established types of political setting. Kerala's village wards are rural, and the earlier village-head studies include southern states. The contrast therefore cannot be reduced to rural versus urban or northern versus southern India. Differences in office, women's educational opportunities, and recruitment into politics remain possible explanations. The overall average and its sensitivity checks are reported in Appendix A; their stability does not explain the differences across settings.

# Discussion

Reservation is associated with a schooling deficit among village heads in the settings we study, while Kerala's village ward members and the councillors of Mumbai and Delhi follow a different pattern. The question is why the schooling gap is smaller in some offices and settings. Differences in women's educational opportunities and selection into politics could explain the contrast. Because location, office, election year and measurement vary together, our evidence does not identify which explanation accounts for it.

\Needspace{4\baselineskip}

Where the education estimates are close to zero, the differences in reported occupation remain large. This pattern is consistent with unequal economic opportunities, but occupation records alone cannot establish who controls resources or exercises the office. In a Rajasthan phone audit, 9% of answered calls to reserved-seat village heads reached the elected woman, against 76% in open seats and 31.7% in urban Jaipur [@karekurvesood, pp. 1–2]. Women elected through quotas participate less in council decisions [@heinze], and surveys in two states find male family members prominent in everyday governance [@amar]. For the same reason, the lower rate of pending cases among urban reserved-seat councillors may overstate the change in the office's criminal exposure: affidavits list the officeholder's own cases, not her relatives', and @karekurvelee [p. 11] note that many Mumbai quota women have male relatives who face charges.

Assessing how qualification differences affect governing performance requires direct measures of officials' behavior. Separate evidence from Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh finds no detectable effect of lottery-assigned reservation on the scale or content of public works [@greensinghsood]. Our administrative records establish differences in who holds office; they cannot establish the consequences of those differences.

# Measurement and reproducibility

## Affidavit verification

We do not use the education recorded in the older Delhi files, whose coding also appears in Karekurve-Ramachandra and Lee's deposit [@localelections; @delhikarekurve]. For the 2012 winners, the deposited graduate classification agrees with the winners' own MyNeta profiles `r fmt(100 * audit$agreement[audit$field == "graduate" & grepl("Delhi", audit$deposit)], 0)`% of the time, close to the agreement obtained after randomly shuffling the deposited values across winners (`r fmt(100 * audit$shuffled[audit$field == "graduate" & grepl("Delhi", audit$deposit)], 0)`%), while the same records' declared assets match `r fmt(100 * audit$agreement[audit$field == "declared assets"], 0)`% of the time. The 2017 education labels agree with the profiles for `r num(delhi_comparison$joint[delhi_comparison$year == 2017] - delhi_comparison$disagreements[delhi_comparison$year == 2017])` of `r num(delhi_comparison$joint[delhi_comparison$year == 2017])` winners. In the Mumbai audit sample, the deposited education and pending-case indicators agree with MyNeta.

## Asset measurement

The asset regressions use $\log(A+1)$, where $A$ is declared assets in rupees. The added rupee retains zero declarations. Percentage differences are $100[\exp(\hat\beta)-1]$, with the same transformation applied to the confidence limits.

## Schooling synthesis

For years of schooling, we divide the reported difference and its standard error by the pooled within-group SD. For binary thresholds, $d=\log(OR)\sqrt{3}/\pi$, and the variance is multiplied by $3/\pi^2$. This is the logistic-distribution conversion in `metafor`'s `OR2DL` measure [@chinn]. Published threshold comparisons use the reported group shares and sizes, with counts rounded to integers. Our comparisons use the reservation coefficient from a fixed-effects logistic regression, with the same controls and clustering as the percentage-point models. Their individual intervals use $t_{G-1}$ critical values. Fixed-effect groups with no outcome variation do not identify the logistic coefficient and are excluded; Table \ref{tab:meta-coverage} reports the resulting coverage.

```{r meta-coverage, results='asis'}
combined$inputs %>%
  filter(source == "This paper") %>%
  transmute(Election = label, `Classified winners` = num(n_input),
            `Logit sample` = num(n), Clusters = num(clusters)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Samples used to standardize this paper's schooling estimates.", label = "meta-coverage", format = table_format,
        booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, longtable = TRUE)
```

The group-summary model is $d_{sj}=\mu_{g(s)}+u_s+v_{sj}+e_{sj}$, where $s$ indexes a published sample or one of our six settings, $j$ indexes an estimate, and $e_{sj}$ has the estimated sampling variance. We estimate both random-effect variances by restricted maximum likelihood and use $t$ intervals with containment degrees of freedom. The mean $\mu_{g(s)}$ distinguishes published village heads, our northern village heads, and our Kerala ward members and city councillors. Sampling errors are assumed independent conditional on the random effects. For comparison, an overall model replaces the group means with one common mean; its sensitivity checks include a sampling-error correlation of 0.5 within settings.

Chattopadhyay and Duflo represent Birbhum in the main pool; Beaman et al. replace them in a sensitivity check. Bamezai et al.'s Table 7, Panel B, column 1 estimates a fuzzy-RD effect near reservation thresholds on winners' education standardized against GP citizens. Column 2 uses a same-gender citizen benchmark; column 3 substitutes husbands' education. None enters our pool: the first has a different target population and standardization, and the others also change the comparison or whose qualifications are measured. Their 2016 Bihar sample overlaps ours; our Bihar estimate is the only one used in the pool. Earlier Delhi and Mumbai deposit-based estimates are not additional independent evidence. Comparisons of women and men, candidate outcomes, and selection relative to citizens are excluded. The pool is drawn from the studies we located and could extract, not a systematic census of the literature. Reconstructed standard errors for published threshold comparisons omit clustering and repeated village observations.

The overall mean is `r fmt(combined_meta$d, 2)` SD (95% CI `r fmt(combined_meta$low, 2)` to `r fmt(combined_meta$high, 2)`), across `r num(combined_meta$estimates)` estimates in `r num(combined_meta$series)` study or setting series. It averages over the assembled comparisons with model-based weights; it is not an average for Indian local offices. Its 95% prediction interval, including both random-effect variances, runs from `r fmt(combined_meta$prediction_low, 2)` to `r fmt(combined_meta$prediction_high, 2)` SD. Omitting each series in turn yields means from `r fmt(min(combined$influence$d), 2)` to `r fmt(max(combined$influence$d), 2)` SD, with all confidence intervals below zero. Table \ref{tab:meta-sensitivity} reports further checks. A stable overall mean is compatible with the distinct setting patterns shown in the main text.

```{r meta-sensitivity, results='asis'}
combined$sensitivity %>%
  transmute(Specification = sub("Within-setting sampling correlation of", "Error correlation:", specification), Estimates = estimates,
            `Difference [95% CI], SD` = paste0(fmt(d, 2), " [", fmt(low, 2), ", ", fmt(high, 2), "]")) %>%
  kable(caption = "Overall schooling average: alternative samples and dependence assumptions.", label = "meta-sensitivity", format = table_format,
        booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, longtable = TRUE)
```

### Additional schooling comparisons from Bhavnani et al.

Table 2 of @bhavnani reports reservation-category coefficients against fully open seats. Within SC/ST-reserved seats, the women's-reservation difference is the SC/ST-women coefficient minus the SC/ST-open coefficient. Table \ref{tab:bhavnani-contrasts} reconstructs these comparisons. The coefficients' covariance is unreported, so the standard error of their difference can range from the absolute difference to the sum of their standard errors. The displayed interval uses that largest standard error and a normal approximation; it is an uncertainty envelope, not an exact reconstructed confidence interval.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

```{r bhavnani-contrasts, results='asis'}
bhavnani %>%
  transmute(Sample = sub("REDS survey", "REDS", sample), Caste = caste,
            Difference = fmt(estimate, 2),
            `SE range` = ifelse(se_low == se_high, fmt(se_low, 2),
                               paste0(fmt(se_low, 2), " to ", fmt(se_high, 2))),
            `95% envelope` = paste0("[", fmt(low, 2), ", ", fmt(high, 2), "]")) %>%
  kable(caption = "Women's-reservation schooling differences in years, reconstructed from Bhavnani et al. (2024), Table 2, columns 4 and 6.", label = "bhavnani-contrasts", format = table_format,
        booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, longtable = TRUE)
```

Odisha uses the 2022 reservation schedule and schooling from the 2011–12 census for matched winners. The other sample comes from the REDS listing survey of 2014–16; the draft does not specify a common election year. The reconstructed differences retain the source's covariate adjustment and matching restrictions. The reported tables lack the schooling SDs needed for standardization and the design information needed to recover our overall caste-adjusted reservation coefficient. We therefore report these results in years and keep them outside the pooled synthesis.

## Coverage and missing outcomes

```{r missingness, results='asis'}
coverage <- bind_rows(lapply(c("uttar_pradesh", "rajasthan", "kerala"), function(state) {
  report$settings[[state]]$descriptive %>% mutate(state = state)
})) %>%
  mutate(State = recode(state, uttar_pradesh = "UP", rajasthan = "Rajasthan", kerala = "Kerala"),
         Office = office_name(tier), Seat = if_else(quota == 1, "Women", "Open"),
         `Classified (%)` = fmt(100 * education_n / n), N = num(n)) %>%
  select(State, Year = year, Office, Seat, `Classified (%)`, N)
kable(coverage, caption = "Education coverage among eligible winner records. N includes unclassified qualifications.",
      booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE)
```

Education is missing for many winners in Rajasthan, where qualifications are often recorded as "Other", and is classified at different rates across Kerala's seat types. Ages outside 21 to 100 are set to missing. Some Uttar Pradesh inputs come from integration work not yet in a published release of the election data; the repository keeps their byte hashes and the adapter diff.

The missing-education bounds keep the all-winner regression design and let each unclassified winner be either a graduate or not. After reservation is residualized on the controls, the coefficient is a weighted sum of outcomes, so assigning each missing outcome by the sign of its weight gives the exact minimum and maximum. The bounds carry no sampling uncertainty. Uttar Pradesh's bounds are negative in each election; Rajasthan's and Kerala's include both signs.

```{r education-bounds, results='asis'}
bound_table <- bounds %>% mutate(
  State = recode(state, uttar_pradesh = "UP", rajasthan = "Rajasthan", kerala = "Kerala"),
  Office = office_name(tier),
  Lower = fmt(all_winners_lower * 100), Upper = fmt(all_winners_upper * 100),
  Missing = num(unclassified), N = num(all_winners_n)
) %>% select(State, Year = year, Office, Lower, Upper, Missing, N)
kable(bound_table, caption = "Missing-education bounds on the adjusted all-winner graduate-share difference (percentage points). These are not confidence intervals.", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE)
```
